_comment: PSEUDO-HEAD: bulk and slab as ONE model, not two.
A dataset that mixes 3D-periodic bulk with 2D-periodic slabs cannot be a
single ordinary head, because `slab_correction` and `pbc` are fixed when
the model is built. But the long-range term holds NO TRAINABLE WEIGHTS --
every parameter lives in the descriptor, the energy head and the charge
head. So one set of weights genuinely serves both; only the sum over
periodic images has to differ.
`same_as` says exactly that. The `slab` branch below IS the `bulk` model
-- the same Python objects, one gradient and one update per step, one set
of per-type energy offsets fitted over both datasets pooled -- carrying a
different long-range term.
CONTRAST WITH EXAMPLE 04. There the three branches came from three levels
of theory with unrelated energy zeros, so they had to be separate heads
sharing only a descriptor. Here there is ONE level of theory and one
system; only the boundary differs. Using `same_as` across different theory
would be wrong, and using separate heads here would waste half the data on
each.
THIS FILE SHIPS NO DATA. Point `data_dict` at your own bulk and slab
subsets -- see the README for what they must have in common.
shared_dict exists here for one reason: DeePMD-kit asserts that a
multi-task model has exactly one SHARED type_map reference. Even a config
whose branches are copies of each other has to name it there.
Nothing else needs a shared_dict entry. `same_as` shares by being the
same model, so there is no list of component names to keep in sync -- and
nothing to forget when the model grows a new part.
The branch that defines the model. Everything here -- descriptor,
fitting net, charge head, type map -- is what BOTH branches run.
rcut must stay below half of the SMALLEST cell in either branch. A
padded slab is tall but usually narrow: check its x/y, not its z.
No dim_case_embd. A case embedding gives each branch its own index in
one buffer, which is precisely the claim `same_as` denies -- so it is
refused rather than silently collapsed.
3D-periodic: no slab correction, no open axis.
mesh spacing must beat 1/(2*alpha) = 1.25 A; size it for THIS cell.
The whole pseudo-head. It may set ONLY `long_range`, plus the optional
`model_branch_alias` and `info`. Writing a descriptor or a fitting_net
here is refused, not ignored: it would be built and then discarded when
the modules are aliased, and training would converge to a model nobody
asked for.
`charge_net` is inherited and cannot be overridden -- it holds weights, so
it must be the same object, not an equal copy.
alpha MUST match the bulk branch. It is where Coulomb is split,
and the one shared descriptor can only learn the erfc(alpha r)/r
remainder of a single split. A mismatch is refused.
The mesh is sized for the PADDED cell, so its z is much larger.
pbc marks z open; slab_correction adds Yeh-Berkowitz, 2 pi Mz^2/V.
Note that correction is IDENTICALLY ZERO for a non-polar slab. If
yours carries no dipole across the vacuum, you do not need this
file at all -- one ordinary 3D branch already serves both.
One loss per branch. Same theory, same weights -- so unless one subset
has virial labels and the other does not, these should be identical.
model_prob is the chance a STEP is drawn from that branch, not a data-size
weight. Slab frames are usually far scarcer and far more expensive than
bulk ones; weight by how much you want each boundary represented in the
gradient, then check both rmse_f columns in lcurve.out actually fall.
_comment_clip: Kept from example 04. The branches share a backbone here too, and a
near-degenerate descriptor coordinate can amplify one branch's gradient
enormously -- clipping is what stops a single step from wrecking weights
